intro.x: **Parliamentary committees** — 'mini-legislatures' — are where scrutiny actually happens, compensating for a House short of time and expertise.

p.x: 24 **Departmentally Related Standing Committees** (since 1993) examine bills, budgets and policy.
**PAC, Estimates and COPU** hold the executive to account on spending, aided by the CAG.
Meetings are closed and off-whip, allowing cross-party, evidence-based examination.
Select, Joint and Committee-of-the-Whole formations handle some scrutiny too.
They bring detailed, technical scrutiny the floor cannot manage in limited hours.
Ministries answer questions and produce data before members across parties.
Reports are usually unanimous, lowering the political temperature of contested issues.
Committees carry continuity and expertise across sessions and governments.
Away from cameras, members engage substance rather than performance.
The share of bills sent to committees has fallen sharply — many major laws pass unscrutinised.
Recommendations are advisory; Action-Taken follow-up is weak.
Low attendance, short member tenures (annual reconstitution) and — unlike the US Congress — no dedicated research staff blunt their edge.
Rising use of ordinances bypasses committee scrutiny of law-making.
Declining sitting days of the House compress the time for committee work.

wf: Make committee reference of bills the norm, build a research secretariat, and enforce attendance and Action-Taken follow-up
gs2-12.conc: Committees are where accountability survives the theatre of the House — bypassing them does not speed law-making, it strips it of scrutiny.

intro.x: **Declining sitting days** and **rising ordinances** signal an executive-heavy legislature — weakening deliberation and accountability.

p.x: Parliament now sits far fewer days than in early decades, compressing scrutiny.
Frequent ordinances legislate without debate, later ratified in bulk.
Disruption and the guillotine push laws and budgets through without discussion.
Erosion of Question Hour and Zero Hour further reduces direct executive answerability.
Fewer sittings squeeze zero-hour and short-duration discussions that surface public concerns.
A strong executive prefers speed over scrutiny.
Disruption becomes an opposition tactic and a government excuse.
No fixed minimum sitting days or independent calendar.
The anti-defection law discourages independent legislative voice, easing government control.
Classifying bills as money bills bypasses the Rajya Sabha and dilutes scrutiny.
Less debate means laws pass unexamined and the House's core deliberative legitimacy erodes.
Ordinances and haste sidestep committee scrutiny.
A guaranteed minimum number of annual sitting days, as the NCRWC and several committees urged.
Judicial and procedural limits on re-promulgation (**Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017**).
A professional, independent legislative research secretariat, like the US Congressional Research Service, would sharpen scrutiny.

wf: Fix a minimum number of sitting days, curb ordinance re-promulgation, and mandate committee reference of bills
gs2-12-b0.conc: A legislature that sits less and legislates by ordinance surrenders its core function — reviving deliberation is essential to parliamentary accountability.

intro.x: Conceived as the federal chamber giving States a voice at the centre, the **Rajya Sabha** has functioned more as a house of revision than a genuine council of States.

p.x: A continuing chamber (**Art 80**), one-third retiring biennially, checks transient majorities.
**Art 249** lets it authorise Union legislation on a State subject; **Art 312** creates All-India Services.
Nomination of eminent persons, and parity with the Lok Sabha in constitutional amendments.

body.h: Why the federal claim falls short

p.x: Unlike the US Senate, States are unequally represented, so it mirrors the popular chamber.
Removal of the residency requirement, upheld in **Kuldip Nayar (2006)**, weakened the State link.
The anti-defection whip makes members vote as partisans rather than as State representatives.
Classifying contested legislation as a money bill sidesteps its scrutiny altogether.

wf: Restore a domicile requirement, free votes on federal questions and stricter money-bill certification.
gs2-13.conc: The chamber revises well but represents States weakly — reform must reconnect the seat to the State it is meant to speak for.

diag.title: Rajya Sabha and the US Senate
diag.foot: India has a second chamber that reproduces, rather than corrects, the demographic asymmetry of the first

intro.x: **Parliamentary privileges** under **Articles 105 and 194** protect the legislature's independence, but being uncodified they sit in uneasy tension with fundamental rights.

p.x: Freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings for anything said or voted.
Beyond enumerated heads, privileges rest on convention rather than statute, leaving contours uncertain.
They exist to protect the House's functioning, not to confer personal advantage on members.
Punishing publication or criticism engages **Art 19(1)(a)**, as the **Keshav Singh** reference (1965) exposed.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)** held expulsion is reviewable — privilege cannot oust the Constitution.
**Sita Soren (2024)** overruled **Narasimha Rao**, denying immunity for bribery linked to a vote.

wf: Codify privileges with defined offences and procedure, so the House's authority and citizens' rights are both certain.
gs2-13-b0.conc: Privilege is a functional shield for the institution, not a sovereign immunity — its future lies in codification, not custom.

intro.x: The **Leader of the Opposition (LoP)** finds no mention in the Constitution, yet has become a statutory linchpin of appointments to India's accountability institutions.

p.x: Recognised by the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition Act, 1977**, with Cabinet rank.
Speaker's Direction practice requires the largest opposition party to hold roughly a tenth of seats.
It institutionalises the opposition as a shadow government and legitimises dissent.
The LoP sits on panels choosing the **Lokpal**, **CBI Director**, **CVC**, **CIC** and **NHRC** members.
No recognised LoP from 2014 to 2024 forced reliance on the single largest party's leader instead.
An absent or weakened LoP dilutes the bipartisan character these appointments were designed to secure.

wf: Anchor recognition in statute on the single-largest-opposition-party basis, so the office cannot lapse for want of a threshold.
gs2-13-b1.conc: The LoP converts opposition from noise into an institutional check — a democracy is poorer when the chair stands empty.

gs2-14.lens: PIL's democratisation of access, its rights and accountability gains, and the overreach/frivolity limits.

intro.x: **Public Interest Litigation** — pioneered by **Bhagwati** and **Krishna Iyer** — relaxed *locus standi* so the court could be reached by those who could not reach it themselves.

p.x: **S.P. Gupta (1981)**: any public-spirited person may move the court for the voiceless.
A letter or postcard could be treated as a writ petition — access without lawyers or fees.
Continuing mandamus, amicus curiae and court-monitored investigations extended the court's reach.
Courts appoint amicus curiae and fact-finding commissions to gather evidence.
**Article 21** was widened — dignity, environment, livelihood.
**Vishaka (1997)** wrote workplace-harassment guidelines where the legislature was silent.
Bonded labour, prisoners and slum-dwellers reached the court through PIL.
PIL built India's environmental law — polluter-pays, precautionary and public-trust doctrines.
Prison, police and custodial-justice reforms flowed from PIL directions.
PIL can slide into governance — courts running administration and setting policy.
Private or political interests dressed as public interest clog the docket.
Sweeping orders often outrun the state's capacity and go unenforced.
Policy-making by court order strains the constitutional division of functions.
Which causes are taken up can appear arbitrary, raising legitimacy concerns.
PIL adds to vast pendency, delaying ordinary litigants.

wf: Filter frivolous PILs with costs, defer on polycentric policy, and keep PIL an instrument of access, not administration
gs2-14.conc: PIL is the court's most democratic instrument and its most contested — its discipline lies in serving access without displacing the elected branches.

intro.x: **Article 142** empowers the Supreme Court to do 'complete justice' — a unique remedial power poised between justice and **overreach**.

p.x: Art 142 lets the Court pass any order necessary for 'complete justice' in a cause before it.
It supplies remedies where statute is silent or inadequate.
Bhopal settlement, cleansing of institutions, and the 2025 'deemed assent' order.
Art 142 works alongside review and curative petitions as an equitable last resort.
It reaches results formal law cannot, protecting rights and public interest.
Used to enforce accountability where other organs failed.
A safety valve for exceptional, unforeseen situations.
It has enforced environmental and custodial-justice norms where the state defaulted.
Used sparingly, it enhances faith that justice will not fail on technicality.
Orders can override express statutory schemes, raising separation-of-powers issues.
'Complete justice' is undefined, inviting inconsistency.
Filling gaps can shade into making policy.
The Court itself cautions that Art 142 cannot override substantive statutory bars.
The Court has held Art 142 cannot be used to contravene express statutory prohibitions.
Clear, reasoned criteria would reduce the charge of ad hoc, unpredictable use.

wf: Exercise Art 142 with reasoned restraint, consistent with statute and separation of powers, reserving it for genuine gaps
gs2-14-b0.conc: Article 142 is the Constitution's instrument of last-resort justice — indispensable in exceptional cases, dangerous if it becomes a routine substitute for law-making.

intro.x: A codified **Memorandum of Procedure (MoP)** would formalise how judges are chosen. The question is whether written criteria discipline the collegium or hand the executive a veto.

p.x: **Second (1993)** and **Third Judges (1998)** cases made judicial primacy the rule; **NJAC** was struck down in 2015.
Opaque criteria, no secretariat and unexplained supersessions invite charges of nepotism.
A revised MoP has remained unsettled since 2015, chiefly over a national-security veto clause.
Published criteria, timelines and reasons strengthen legitimacy without transferring the choice.
An open-ended executive objection, or indefinite delay in notifying names, is a veto by inaction.
A permanent secretariat, declared merit-and-diversity criteria and binding timelines on both sides.

wf: Finalise the MoP with objective criteria and enforceable timelines, while excluding an unreviewable executive veto.
gs2-15.conc: Independence and transparency are complements, not rivals — a reasoned, time-bound process protects the judiciary better than secrecy does.

diag.title: Judicial independence — four legs
rows: court budget voted by the State
MoP unsettled; staff, infra with State
diag.foot: Independence contested only at appointment leaves the daily dependence untouched

intro.x: **Administrative tribunals** were meant to deliver speedy, expert and cheap justice, but decades on they have added a tier without displacing the courts.

p.x: Inserted by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**; the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** created the **CAT**.
Expert members and flexible procedure suit technical, high-volume service and regulatory disputes.
Focused jurisdiction was expected to relieve High Courts of routine service litigation.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** preserved High Court review under **Art 226** as basic structure, so appeals persist.
Appointments, tenure and funding controlled by the parent ministry — often the litigant — compromise impartiality.
Chronic vacancies, weak infrastructure and repeated litigation over the **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** erode speed.

wf: Establish an independent **National Tribunals Commission** for appointments, funding and oversight, with fixed tenure and filled benches.
gs2-16.conc: Tribunals fail not in conception but in insulation — expert justice needs independence from the executive it is asked to judge.

gs2-17.lens: Judicial review in India vs the US: due process vs procedure established by law, and India's wider but distinct model.

intro.x: Both India and the United States practise **judicial review**, but on different textual foundations and with different reach.

p.x: **Marbury v Madison (1803)** inferred review from the Constitution's supremacy — it is not expressly granted.
The **'due process of law'** (5th/14th Amendments) lets courts test the substance and fairness of laws.
A rigid separation of powers and strong individual-rights review.
US review strongly shields entrenched individual rights against legislative majorities.
US courts avoid 'political questions', deferring to the elected branches.
**Articles 13, 32 and 226** expressly empower courts to strike down unconstitutional laws and acts.
**Article 21** borrowed the narrower Japanese phrase — later widened by interpretation.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** read due-process in through **Articles 14, 19 and 21** together.
India uniquely reviews constitutional amendments themselves — absent in the US.
PIL gives Indian review a reach into governance the American model lacks.
Basic-structure review and PIL make Indian review broader than the American.
India balances rights against **DPSP** and social goals; the US leans harder on individual rights.
Indian courts are often more deferential on economic policy than on personal liberty.
US judges are politically appointed and confirmed; India evolved the collegium.
Both increasingly weigh proportionality and reasonableness in rights adjudication.

gs2-17.conc: India adopted the mechanism of judicial review but on its own terms — express, wider in scope through basic structure and PIL, and disciplined by the balance with directive goals.
flash: India wider via basic structure + PIL

intro.x: India inherited the **Westminster** parliamentary model but adapted it to a **federal, written and rights-based** constitution — a distinctive departure.

p.x: A Cabinet drawn from and answerable to the legislature.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
A constitutional head (President) acting on ministerial advice; bicameralism; Speaker's role.
An impartial Speaker and a revising second chamber are core inherited features.
Unlike the UK's unwritten conventions, India codified powers and limits.
A dual polity with distributed powers, unknown to unitary Britain.
A written bill of rights enforceable by courts — parliamentary supremacy replaced by constitutional supremacy.
Even amendments are limited — no equivalent in the UK.
Non-justiciable DPSP graft a welfare-state vision onto the Westminster form.
Universal adult suffrage from the outset was a bold departure from gradual British enfranchisement.
India blends Westminster form with American-style constitutionalism.
A strong Centre with federal features — 'cooperative federalism'.
Fundamental Rights and remedies (Arts 32/226) anchor the departure.
The model is adapted continuously to Indian diversity and scale.
A single integrated judiciary, unlike the US dual system, is an Indian innovation.
Elaborate emergency provisions have no Westminster parallel.

wf: Retain Westminster accountability while deepening the federal and rights-based features that distinguish the Indian model
gs2-17-b0.conc: India took Westminster's parliamentary government but rejected its parliamentary supremacy — grafting it onto a federal, written and justiciable constitution of its own making.

intro.x: **Article 19(1)(a)** jurisprudence has moved from protecting the speaker to governing platforms — scale, virality and intermediary power now define the free-speech question.

p.x: **Kaushal Kishor (2023)** held no restriction beyond the eight grounds in **Art 19(2)** may be imposed.
**Shreya Singhal (2015)** voided **Section 66A** and read down intermediary liability as chilling speech.
**Anuradha Bhasin (2020)** made internet shutdowns subject to necessity, proportionality and publication.
Misinformation and coordinated amplification cause harm that a pre-digital doctrine never anticipated.
A government **Fact Check Unit** as arbiter of its own affairs was struck down by the Bombay High Court (2024).
Opaque takedowns and algorithmic ranking curtail reach without any constitutional standard applying.
Narrow definitions, notice, appeal and transparency reports serve better than broad blocking powers.

wf: Legislate narrowly-defined harms with independent adjudication, mandatory transparency and a right of appeal against takedown.
gs2-19.conc: The remedy for harmful speech in a constitutional democracy remains more speech and due process — not a wider power to silence.

intro.x: The replacement of **Section 124A IPC** by **Section 152 BNS** was presented as abolishing sedition, but the successor provision is in substance wider, not narrower.

p.x: **124A** punished disaffection towards government; **Kedar Nath Singh (1962)** saved it by limiting it to incitement to violence.
The Supreme Court paused all proceedings under 124A in 2022 pending reconsideration.
**Section 152 BNS** penalises acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, with up to life imprisonment.
'Subversive activities' and 'encouraging separatist feelings' extend beyond the violence test Kedar Nath required.
Undefined terms leave the same scope for chilling dissent that made the colonial section objectionable.
Only a statutory incitement-to-imminent-violence threshold, and sanction before FIR, would mark a genuine break.

wf: Codify the Kedar Nath violence threshold into Section 152 and require prior sanction, so criticism is not criminalised.
gs2-19-b0.conc: The name has gone but the grip remains — repeal is meaningful only when the successor is narrower than what it replaced.

intro.x: Since **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** read fairness into 'procedure established by law', **Article 21** has grown into the Constitution's most generative right, absorbing new claims of dignity.

p.x: **Puttaswamy (2017)** located informational and decisional privacy within life and liberty.
**Common Cause (2018)** recognised passive euthanasia and advance directives as part of a dignified life.
**M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024)** read a right against the adverse effects of climate change into **Arts 21 and 14**.
Rights are inferred from dignity, then made enforceable through directions and continuing mandamus.
Judicially created entitlements without budgets raise separation-of-powers and enforceability concerns.
Expansion is meaningful only when it reaches undertrials, the displaced and the destitute, not merely the articulate.

wf: Convert judicially recognised entitlements into statutory schemes with funding and grievance redress, so declaration becomes delivery.
gs2-20.conc: Article 21's horizon expands because dignity is not exhaustible — the test is whether the promise reaches those least able to claim it.

intro.x: **Preventive detention** — imprisonment without trial on suspicion — is constitutionally sanctioned by **Article 22**, making India unusual among democracies in permitting it in peacetime.

p.x: **Art 22(3)-(7)** excludes detenus from the ordinary safeguards of arrest and counsel that Art 22(1)-(2) give.
Detention beyond three months needs an **Advisory Board**; grounds must be communicated and representation allowed.
**Ameena Begum (2023)** reiterated that such laws are an exception, to be applied with rigour, not routine.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** laid down arrest memos, medical examination and information to relatives.
**Nilabati Behera (1993)** made the State liable in public law for custodial death.
Routine invocation of **NSA/UAPA**, delayed board review and weak prosecution of custodial violence blunt these protections.

wf: Require recorded reasons, time-bound judicial review of every detention and independent investigation of custodial deaths.
gs2-20-b0.conc: Liberty's exception must not become the rule — preventive detention is defensible only under a discipline the ordinary law never needs.

gs2-21.lens: Harmonious construction of FRs and DPSP; the conflict history and their reading as complementary.

intro.x: **Fundamental Rights** (justiciable) and **Directive Principles** (non-justiciable) are complementary — the doctrine of **harmonious construction** reads them together rather than in conflict.

p.x: **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** held FRs prevail — prompting the **First Amendment** (Arts 15(4), 31A/B).
The **25th Amendment**'s Art 31C shielded laws implementing certain DPSP from FR challenge.
**Kesavananda (1973)** limited 31C; **Minerva Mills (1980)** held the FR-DPSP **balance** itself part of the basic structure.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** widened Art 31C to all DPSP — later read down.
Courts avoid any reading that renders either FRs or DPSP nugatory.
Directive Principles guide the interpretation of Fundamental Rights and the reasonableness of restrictions.
DPSP enriched Art 21 — education (**Unnikrishnan** → **86th Amendment, Art 21A**), health and environment.
DPSP justify reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights in the public interest.
FRs and DPSP are the 'two wheels of the chariot' — liberty and welfare together.
DPSP are the aims; FRs the means and limits — read as one scheme.
The balance shifts with context but neither may be extinguished.
Courts convert directives into enforceable standards via Art 21 — food, shelter, health.
Neither is superior; the Constitution is read as a whole to give effect to both.
Socio-economic and environmental rights rest on the FR-DPSP synthesis.

wf: Read FRs and DPSP as a single scheme — using DPSP to interpret rights and justify reasonable, welfare-oriented restrictions
gs2-21.conc: The FR-DPSP relationship models the constitutional balance between liberty and social welfare — harmonious construction is how the document holds both without sacrificing either.

intro.x: **Article 32** and **Article 226** both provide writ remedies, but differ in status, scope and reach.

p.x: Art 32 is itself a Fundamental Right — Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Enforceable only against violation of Fundamental Rights, before the Supreme Court.
Its guarantee cannot ordinarily be denied.
Under Art 32, standing was relaxed via PIL, widening access to the apex court.
Art 226 is a power of High Courts, not a fundamental right.
It runs for Fundamental Rights *and* 'any other purpose' — including legal rights.
Enforceable where the cause of action arises, giving High Courts broad supervisory jurisdiction.
High Courts may decline Art 226 relief where an efficacious alternative exists.
Art 226 is wider (any legal right); Art 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights.
High Courts have more discretion to refuse relief than the Supreme Court under Art 32.
Exhaustion of Art 226 before Art 32 is often encouraged to avoid crowding the apex court.
Together they make rights meaningfully enforceable at two levels.
Dismissal on merits under one can bar the other, preventing forum-shopping.
Both issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

wf: Encourage recourse to Art 226 first for wider grievances, reserving Art 32 for direct Fundamental-Rights violations
gs2-21-b0.conc: Article 32 guarantees the remedy that makes rights real, while Article 226 casts a wider supervisory net — together they anchor India's rights-enforcement architecture.

gs2-22.lens: Indian secularism as 'principled distance' (Bhargava) — not a wall of separation; its constitutional basis and tensions.

intro.x: Indian secularism is not strict separation but **'principled distance'** (**Rajeev Bhargava**) — the state keeps a context-sensitive distance from all religions, intervening or abstaining as justice requires.

p.x: Unlike the US, the state may **engage** religion — reforming it or supporting it even-handedly.
The Constitution empowers intervention against oppressive practice.
**Sarva dharma sambhava** — equal respect, not rigid equidistance, is the ideal.
The state may fund and regulate endowments and pilgrimages even-handedly.
Distance is calibrated — closer for reform, further for autonomy.
**Articles 25-28** guarantee conscience, practice and propagation, subject to public order and reform.
**Articles 14-15** and the **Preamble** ('secular', 42nd Amendment) anchor non-discrimination.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** held secularism part of the **basic structure**.
Religious freedom is subject to public order, morality, health and other rights.
The **Essential Religious Practices** doctrine draws courts into deciding what is 'essential' to a faith.
**Article 44** and personal-law reform test the balance between rights and community autonomy.
Even-handedness is strained where the state's neutrality is politically contested.
Reforming personal laws tests equality against community autonomy.
Legitimacy rests on treating all faiths alike, in both support and restraint.

wf: Anchor secularism in even-handed treatment and reform, minimising judicial definition of religion and protecting minority rights
gs2-22.conc: Principled distance lets a deeply religious society be secular on its own terms — its coherence tested constantly by the even-handedness of the state.
flash: no wall of separation; Art 17 reform

intro.x: The **Essential Religious Practices (ERP)** doctrine lets courts decide what a religion 'essentially' requires — protecting faith yet inviting critique.

p.x: Evolved from **Shirur Mutt (1954)** — only 'essential' practices get Art 25/26 protection.
To separate protected religious cores from mere superstition or secular activity.
Applied in Ananda Margi, Shayara Bano and Sabarimala to test claims of religious right.
Art 26 protects a denomination's right to manage its own religious affairs.
Judges decide doctrinal essentiality — a role they are ill-suited to.
Outcomes vary, making the test unpredictable.
It can override community practice in the name of reform, or entrench it.
Judicial essentiality tests can freeze internal reform within communities.
Even-handed treatment, not indifference, is the test of Indian state neutrality.
Some urge shifting from 'essentiality' to whether a practice violates dignity/equality.
Bhargava/Sen-style focus on harm and exclusion rather than doctrine.
Protect faith but subordinate practices that violate Fundamental Rights.
The larger-bench reference on ERP may recalibrate the doctrine.
Reform (Sabarimala, triple talaq) pits equality against religious autonomy.
A nine-judge bench is reconsidering the doctrine's scope and limits.

wf: Move from judging doctrinal 'essentiality' to testing practices against dignity, equality and the anti-exclusion principle
gs2-22-b0.conc: The ERP doctrine draws courts into theology they should avoid — the sounder path is to protect religious freedom while testing practice against constitutional values, not scripture.

intro.x: The **right to vote** is a constitutional/statutory right, not a Fundamental Right — a status with real consequences for its protection.

p.x: Rooted in **Article 326** and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 — not in Part III.
**Kuldip Nayar** and others held it a statutory (constitutional) right, though a minority sees it as near-fundamental.
Being non-fundamental, it is more amenable to legislative regulation and restriction.
Universal adult franchise (Art 326) is itself part of the basic structure.
Qualifications, disqualifications and procedures can be set by ordinary law.
It lacks Art 32 protection as a Fundamental Right, though Art 226 remains available.
**PUCL** located voting's *expression* (NOTA, disclosure) within Art 19(1)(a).
Courts expanded voter rights — NOTA, candidate disclosure — via Art 19(1)(a).
The **Election Commission (Art 324)** superintends rolls and elections.
Transparent revision, notice and appeal against deletion; roll revision (SIR) must avoid arbitrary mass deletion of eligible voters.
Arbitrary disenfranchisement is challengeable for violating Arts 14/21.
Special efforts for the marginalised, migrants and first-time voters; remote-voting and portability reforms aim to include migrant workers.
Blanket disenfranchisement of undertrials is contested as disproportionate.

wf: Strengthen transparent, appealable electoral-roll procedures under an independent EC to prevent arbitrary exclusion
gs2-23-b0.conc: Voting's statutory status makes robust institutional safeguards — an independent Commission and fair roll procedures — the true guarantee of the franchise.

intro.x: The **Comptroller and Auditor-General** is the constitutional auditor of the public purse, but new financing routes — PPPs, SPVs and off-budget borrowing — increasingly fall outside its reach.

p.x: **Arts 148-151**: appointed by the President, removable only like a Supreme Court judge, salary charged on the Consolidated Fund.
Audits Union and State receipts and expenditure, and bodies substantially financed from public funds.
Reports go to the legislature and feed the **PAC** and **COPU** — audit supplies evidence, committees the consequence.
Private concessionaires and special-purpose vehicles resist audit, though public risk and assets are involved.
Borrowing through parastatals keeps liabilities outside the accounts audit examines.
Delayed tabling weakens relevance, and executive-controlled selection invites doubts about independence.
Action-taken replies are late and non-binding, so findings rarely change administrative behaviour.

wf: Extend audit to PPP concessions and off-budget entities, and set statutory action-taken timelines.
gs2-25.conc: Audit is only as strong as its reach and its consequence — the guardian of the purse must follow public money wherever it now travels.

intro.x: The **Lokpal** and the **NHRC** were created to hold power accountable, yet both largely inquire and recommend — the charge that they lack teeth is only partly deserved.

p.x: The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013** covers the Prime Minister with safeguards, but the first appointment came only in 2019.
It relies on the **CBI** and **CVC** for investigation, so its reach is only as strong as theirs.
Under the **PHRA, 1993** it can inquire and recommend but not enforce, with limited reach over the armed forces.
Publicity, reasoned findings and compensation recommendations shape conduct even without binding power.
Vacancies, thin investigative staff and delayed or formal action-taken replies hollow out both institutions.
Deferral of the NHRC's **GANHRI 'A' status** review flagged concerns about autonomy and pluralism in composition.

wf: Fill vacancies promptly, give both bodies independent investigative capacity and impose a statutory duty to respond to recommendations.
gs2-26.conc: Teeth matter less than independence and follow-through — an accountability body earns authority when its findings reliably attract consequence.

diag.title: Accountability institutions and what each lacks
diag.foot: each institution is given a power and denied the one that would make it work
diag.note: three rows — the pattern is the argument

intro.x: The **Fifth** and **Sixth Schedules** both protect tribal areas, but they embody different philosophies: protective administration by the Governor versus genuine self-government through elected councils.

p.x: **Art 244(1)** covers Scheduled Areas in ten States; the Governor may modify laws, advised by a **Tribes Advisory Council**.
**Art 244(2)** covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram through **Autonomous District Councils**.
ADCs hold legislative, executive, judicial and financial powers; the Fifth Schedule confers only protection.
TACs are advisory and irregular, and Governors rarely exercise the power to modify laws.
**PESA, 1996** vested Gram Sabhas with control over minor minerals, produce and consent, but State rules dilute it.
Councils face financial dependence, delayed elections and friction with State governments.
**Xaxa Committee (2014)**: make TAC advice binding, implement PESA in letter and extend real devolution.

wf: Give Tribes Advisory Councils binding voice, enforce PESA consent and devolve funds and functionaries to autonomous councils.
gs2-27.conc: Protection without power is paternalism — tribal self-governance advances only when consent and control rest with the community.

intro.x: Indian citizenship rests on **Part II** of the Constitution and the **Citizenship Act, 1955**, a framework built on jus soli that successive amendments have moved toward descent and religion.

p.x: **Arts 5-11** settled citizenship at commencement and left the subject to Parliament.
Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory under the 1955 Act.
The 1986 and 2003 amendments required a citizen parent, and introduced the 'illegal migrant' category.
Fast-tracked naturalisation for six non-Muslim communities from three neighbours, with a 2014 cut-off — challenged under **Art 14**.
**Section 6A**, upheld by a Constitution Bench in 2024, sets the 1971 Assam Accord cut-off.
NRC experience showed that proving descent falls hardest on the poor, women and the undocumented, risking statelessness.

wf: Anchor eligibility in secular, verifiable criteria with accessible appeals, and legislate a statutory refugee law distinct from citizenship.
gs2-28.conc: Citizenship defines who belongs; a framework that turns on religion or paperwork risks excluding the very people it should protect.

intro.x: The abrogation of **Article 370** in August 2019 and the downgrading of a State into two Union Territories raised questions that reach beyond Jammu and Kashmir into the design of Indian federalism.

p.x: **Art 370** was rendered inoperative and the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019** created two Union Territories.
**In Re Article 370 (2023)** held the provision temporary and the abrogation valid.
The Court ordered Assembly elections and restoration of statehood at the earliest — polls followed in 2024.
Converting a State into a Union Territory without its legislature's concurrence is the precedent that unsettles States.
Special arrangements under **Arts 371A-371J** rest on similar guarantees, so the reasoning resonates wider.
Statehood restoration is the test of whether reorganisation was a security measure or a permanent demotion.

wf: Restore full statehood on a declared timeline, and require legislative concurrence before converting a State into a UT.
gs2-28-b0.conc: Federalism is tested not by the powers the Union holds but by the restraint with which it uses them — the promise of statehood must be kept.

intro.x: **Section 17A** of the Prevention of Corruption Act requires prior approval before investigating decisions taken by a public servant in official discharge — a shield for honest officers that risks sheltering the corrupt.

p.x: No inquiry into any recommendation or decision made in official functions may begin without competent-authority approval.
Post-2G, fear of prosecution for bona fide commercial judgment produced decision paralysis in administration.
**Section 19** separately requires sanction before a court takes cognisance for prosecution.
The authority granting approval is often the very government whose decisions are in question.
Absent statutory timelines, evidence goes cold while approval is awaited.
17A does not apply to on-the-spot bribery, so trap cases proceed — the gap lies in decision-based corruption.

wf: Impose a fixed timeline with deemed approval, require reasoned refusals and vest the decision in an independent authority.
gs2-28-b1.conc: Honest officers deserve protection from vexatious prosecution, but a safeguard without timelines becomes immunity by delay.

intro.x: Grievance redress is where the citizen actually meets the State. Platforms like **CPGRAMS** convert a scattered complaint culture into a traceable, time-bound system — the raw material of trust.

p.x: Every grievance gets a number, an owner and a deadline, replacing discretion with an audit trail.
AI-assisted routing, regional-language interfaces and voice access reach citizens paper systems missed.
Complaint clustering reveals systemic failure, not just individual cases — diagnosis, not merely disposal.
Closure rates rose faster than satisfaction; a case shut without remedy deepens cynicism.
Field officials who must actually fix the problem are often outside the digital loop.
The digitally excluded — elderly, poor, remote — still depend on intermediaries.
Without independent appeal and accountability for repeat failure, the platform records grievances rather than settling them.

wf: Audit quality of redress rather than disposal speed, add independent appeal, and feed recurring complaints into scheme redesign.
gs2-33.conc: Technology can make the State reachable; only resolution and consequence make it trustworthy.

intro.x: **Mission Karmayogi** shifts civil-service development from rules to roles — defining what competencies a post requires. It addresses capability, but the rigidities it must overcome are structural.

p.x: **FRAC** maps roles, activities and competencies, giving a common language for training and posting.
A **Capacity Building Commission** standardises content and audits outcomes; **iGOT** delivers learning at scale.
It targets attitude and domain depth, not merely procedural knowledge.
Training changes nothing while transfers remain seniority- and preference-driven.
Domain capability cannot accumulate under short, arbitrary tenures unless appraisal rewards it.
The **AIS** is a fraction of the workforce; State and cutting-edge staff carry most citizen contact.
Rule-bound risk aversion persists while honest error is punished more surely than inaction.

wf: Bind deployment to competency, assure minimum tenure, and extend the framework to State and frontline cadres.
gs2-34.conc: Capacity building is necessary but not sufficient — capability grows only where the incentive structure lets it be used.

intro.x: **Lateral entry** brings domain specialists into senior posts long held by career generalists. The two can coexist — provided entry is merit-based and the service builds depth of its own.

p.x: Short tenures across unrelated sectors leave the Secretariat structurally shallow in finance, technology and climate.
External entry widens perspective and ends the career service's monopoly over senior advice.
Most mature administrations combine a career policy cadre with specialist entry at senior levels.
Career officers see promotion narrowed; selection outside the regular process invites charges of patronage.
Recruitment must respect constitutional equality and legitimate concerns about reservation and diversity.
**UPSC**-run transparent selection, conflict-of-interest and cooling-off rules, and structured induction.
Build domain streams and mid-career specialisation, as the **2nd ARC** urged, so expertise grows inside too.

wf: Use lateral entry for genuinely scarce expertise through UPSC-administered selection, while building domain streams within the service.
gs2-34-b0.conc: Lateral entry supplements a career service; it cannot substitute for building depth inside it.

intro.x: Police reform in India is not short of blueprints — the **National Police Commission**, **Prakash Singh (2006)** and the **2nd ARC** all prescribed the same cure. Implementation is the missing element.

p.x: **State Security Commissions** to set policy and shield the force from illegitimate direction.
Fixed minimum tenure for the DGP and field officers, with merit-based selection.
Investigation separated from law and order, and **Police Establishment Boards** for transfers.
**Police Complaints Authorities** for misconduct, replacing internal inquiry alone.
Entry 2, List II means the Union can persuade but not compel; State compliance has been nominal.
Control over postings and cases is a resource no government surrenders willingly.
Model-Act adoption often omits independence, tenure and external complaint mechanisms.

wf: Legislate genuine State Security Commissions and complaints authorities, with judicial monitoring of compliance and funded modernisation.
gs2-35.conc: The diagnosis has been settled for decades; reform now depends on political will, not further commissions.

intro.x: India has multiplied sector regulators without securing their autonomy. The **Data Protection Board** under the **DPDP Act, 2023** illustrates the pattern: a new body, an old dependence.

p.x: Composition, terms and service conditions set by the executive make the regulator answerable to its overseer.
Reliance on government budgets rather than a statutory fund constrains independent action.
Where government is itself the largest data fiduciary or service provider, broad exemptions blunt oversight.
Sectoral expertise and data that regulators need are often held by the entities they regulate — inviting **regulatory capture**.
Collegial, transparent appointment with fixed tenure and protection from arbitrary removal.
Answerability through parliamentary committees, published reasons and judicial review — not ministerial direction.
A specialised, adequately staffed appellate tier prevents regulatory decisions from being litigated into irrelevance.

wf: Legislate insulated appointments, independent funding and narrow, reasoned State exemptions, with parliamentary rather than executive accountability.
gs2-36.conc: A regulator without autonomy transfers discretion rather than disciplining it — independence is the whole point of the fourth branch.

diag.title: A regulator's three hats
diag.foot: separation must be supplied by **procedure**: consultation + reasons · separated adjudicatory wing · fixed non-renewable tenure · appeal + Art 226 review (**L. Chandra Kumar**)

gs2-39.lens: Genuine decentralisation needs the three Fs — Functions, Funds, Functionaries — not just elected local bodies.

intro.x: **Genuine decentralisation** requires devolving the three Fs — **Functions, Funds and Functionaries** — not merely holding local elections.

p.x: The **73rd and 74th Amendments** created elected Panchayats and Municipalities with fixed terms.
The **11th and 12th Schedules** list 29 and 18 subjects for devolution (Art 243G, 243W).
**State Finance Commissions** and **District Planning Committees** were mandated to resource and plan locally.
The Gram Sabha is the constitutional site of direct participatory democracy.
Reserved seats for women (a third to a half) and SC/ST deepen representation.
Subjects are on paper; real authority is retained by line departments and parallel bodies.
Own revenue is weak, grants are tied, and **State Finance Commissions** are often ignored or delayed.
Staff are on deputation and answer upward, not to the elected local council.
Line-department societies and missions bypass elected local governments.
Clearly assign each function to a tier, with matching authority.
Untied grants (as the **15th FC** local grants attempt) and buoyant own-source revenue.
A dedicated local-government cadre and empowered DPCs/MPCs; the **State** is the real bottleneck.
Property tax, user charges and local cess must be tapped to cut dependence.
eGramSwaraj, data and training build local administrative capability.
Devolution varies sharply — Kerala and Karnataka lead, others lag.

wf: Devolve all three Fs through activity mapping, untied finance, a local cadre and empowered planning committees
gs2-39.conc: A three-tier structure exists on paper; without the three Fs it is decentralisation in form and centralisation in substance.

intro.x: India's experiment with **decentralised planning** promised bottom-up development but has struggled to bridge intent and ground outcomes.

p.x: Arts 243G/243ZD envisage local planning through DPCs and MPCs.
The **People's Plan Campaign (1996)** devolved a large plan share to local bodies.
Gram Sabha-led plans to match schemes to local need.
Local plans were to integrate schemes around a shared district outcome.
Effective plans map local needs first, then match schemes — an Elmore-style logic.
District and Metropolitan Planning Committees are often un-constituted or nominal.
Centrally/State-designed schemes crowd out genuine local planning.
Local bodies lack planning skills, data and untied funds.
Plans can reflect dominant interests, not the marginalised.
Scheme-tied funds prevent local bodies from planning holistically.
Better-staffed States plan credibly; weaker ones default to line-department plans.
Constitute and empower DPCs to integrate rural-urban plans.
Discretionary resources make local planning meaningful.
GIS, data and training (as in Kerala) enable credible plans.
Active Gram Sabhas and social audit anchor accountability.
GIS-based planning (as in Kerala) grounds plans in local geography.
MPCs must integrate peri-urban growth ignored by siloed planning.

wf: Empower DPCs/MPCs, provide untied funds and planning capacity, and root plans in active Gram Sabhas
gs2-39-b0.conc: Decentralised planning fails not in design but in delivery — bridging intent and outcome needs empowered committees, untied funds and genuine participation.

intro.x: With the **Smart Cities Mission** concluded, urban reform must return to the unfinished agenda of the **74th Amendment**: Urban Local Bodies that actually hold functions, funds and functionaries.

p.x: **Twelfth Schedule** functions remain with State parastatals — development authorities, water and transport boards.
Own revenues are thin; property tax is under-assessed and **State Finance Commission** devolution is irregular.
Municipal cadres lack engineers, planners and accountants; posts of even municipal commissioner are often in flux.
**SPV**-led mission structures delivered projects while bypassing elected councils.
Transfer Twelfth Schedule functions with staff, and make parastatals accountable to the council.
Reform property-tax assessment and enable municipal bonds and land-value capture for creditworthy cities.
A directly elected mayor with a fixed term, supported by a professional municipal cadre.

wf: Make State Finance Commission devolution timely and formula-based, and tie central funds to genuine functional transfer.
gs2-40.conc: Cities cannot be governed by project vehicles — a mission builds assets, but only an empowered local government sustains them.

intro.x: Tribal welfare has moved from protection to saturation delivery, yet the **75 PVTG** communities — the most vulnerable — remain hardest to reach precisely because generic schemes assume documentation and demand.

p.x: **FRA, 2006** recognises individual and community forest rights; **PESA, 1996** vests Gram Sabhas with consent powers.
**PM-JANMAN** for PVTG habitations and **Dharti Aaba (PM-JUGA)** for saturation of tribal villages.
**Eklavya Model Residential Schools**, MSP for forest produce and the **Tribal Sub-Plan** for earmarked funds.
PVTG settlements are small, remote and mobile; schemes designed for villages miss them entirely.
Community forest rights and habitat rights are sparsely recognised, and consent is often manufactured.
Mining and infrastructure in Fifth Schedule areas remain the largest source of dispossession.
Vacancies in tribal-area posts and language barriers weaken health, nutrition and education access.

wf: Settle habitat and community forest rights first, fund habitation-level delivery, and enforce genuine Gram Sabha consent.
gs2-43.conc: Saturation works only where entitlement is secure — for PVTGs, recognising rights is itself the most effective welfare intervention.

intro.x: The **NFSA, 2013** made food a legal entitlement for about two-thirds of Indians. It has largely ended hunger of the acute kind, but calorie sufficiency is not nutrition security.

p.x: Subsidised grain as a right, with the **PDS** covering roughly 80 crore people and priority to women as household head.
End-to-end computerisation, Aadhaar-linked ration cards and **One Nation One Ration Card** portability for migrants.
**PMGKAY** demonstrated the system's capacity to absorb a nationwide shock.
Cereal-centric rations neglect protein and micronutrients — the **malnutrition paradox** of stunting amid sufficiency.
Coverage still rests on 2011 census population, excluding a decade's additions.
Authentication failure and documentation gaps deny the most mobile and destitute.
Open-ended cereal procurement skews cropping toward water-intensive rice and wheat.

wf: Diversify the basket toward millets and pulses, update coverage to current population, and add fortification with cash-plus options.
gs2-44.conc: The Act settled the right to food; the next step is a right to nutrition — measured in outcomes, not in tonnes distributed.

intro.x: India's **malnutrition paradox** — stunting and anaemia persisting alongside food sufficiency and rising incomes — is what **POSHAN Abhiyaan** and **Mission Saksham Anganwadi** were designed to attack.

p.x: POSHAN Abhiyaan aligns health, ICDS, water and sanitation around measurable stunting and anaemia targets.
**Poshan Tracker** captures growth measurement and service delivery at the anganwadi in real time.
Focus on the first 1,000 days, adolescent girls and lactating mothers, where deficits become irreversible.
**NFHS-5** shows sanitation, maternal education, birth spacing and anaemia matter as much as calories.
Honorarium-based workers carry survey, delivery and data duties with thin infrastructure.
Cereal-heavy consumption leaves protein and micronutrient gaps that supplementation alone cannot close.
Tracking growth matters only where faltering triggers referral and follow-up.

wf: Invest in anganwadi infrastructure and worker capability, diversify the food basket, and link growth-faltering data to guaranteed referral.
gs2-44-b0.conc: Nutrition is an outcome of many systems, not one scheme — India will close the gap by treating it as a determinant problem, not a delivery problem.

gs2-46.lens: The proliferation of commissions for vulnerable sections — overlapping mandates, weak powers, and the case for coherence.

intro.x: A **multiplicity of statutory commissions** for vulnerable sections raises problems of overlap, inconsistency and diffused accountability.

p.x: **NCSC (Art 338)**, **NCST (338A)** and **NCBC (338B, 102nd Amendment)** oversee SC, ST and backward classes.
**NCW, NCM, NCPCR** and others cover women, minorities and children.
Largely **recommendatory** powers, dependence on a parent ministry, and civil-court-like inquiry functions.
They advise on policy, safeguard rights and inquire into complaints of denial.
Within their mandate they have powers of summons and evidence.
Intersectional cases — a Dalit woman, a minority child — fall between mandates.
Constitutional commissions have more teeth than statutory ones; standards are inconsistent.
Recommendations are non-binding; vacancies and thin secretariats blunt them.
Overlaps with the **NHRC** and among themselves dilute rather than concentrate protection.
Members are often political nominees, weakening independence.
Weak disaggregated data limits monitoring of outcomes for each group.
Better coordination — a clear division of labour and referral protocol with the NHRC.
End vacancies, standardise powers and add binding follow-up.
Design for overlapping vulnerabilities rather than single-axis mandates.
Clear referral protocols with the NHRC would cut overlap.
Binding follow-up and Action-Taken reporting would give recommendations force.

wf: Rationalise mandates, standardise powers, fill vacancies and build intersectional, coordinated protection under a coherent architecture
gs2-46.conc: Many guardians can mean diffused guardianship — the vulnerable are protected by coherence and enforcement, not by the multiplication of commissions.

intro.x: Pandemic preparedness cannot be built inside the health department alone. **One Health** recognises that most emerging infections are zoonotic, so human, animal and environmental surveillance must be one system.

body.h: Why One Health is the frame

p.x: Most emerging infections cross from animals — Nipah, avian influenza, COVID-19.
**IDSP/IHIP**, animal-husbandry and wildlife reporting must share data to detect spillover early.
A **National One Health Mission** and the **National Institute of One Health** aim to join these silos.
The colonial **Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897** needs replacement with a rights-respecting public-health law.
A dedicated cadre with epidemiologists at district level, absent in most States.
Health and wellness centres plus a tiered laboratory network — detection happens locally or not at all.
Health is a State subject; standing Centre-State protocols must replace crisis-time improvisation.

wf: Enact a modern public-health Act, build a district public-health cadre and integrate human, animal and environmental surveillance.
gs2-47.conc: Resilience is built between outbreaks, not during them — surveillance, cadre and law are the investments that decide the next response.

diag.title: The pandemic bargain
diag.foot: sharing is immediate, benefit is deferred — without an enforceable return leg the first country withholds
diag.note: a loop with a weak return arrow

intro.x: **Ayushman Bharat** pairs **PM-JAY** hospitalisation cover with **Health and Wellness Centres**, but universal health coverage requires more than insuring the poor against catastrophic bills.

p.x: PM-JAY offers **₹5 lakh** annual cover per family, extended to all citizens aged 70 and above.
**Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** shift the model from selective to comprehensive primary care.
**ABDM** health IDs and registries aim to make records portable across providers.
Insurance covers hospitalisation, while outpatient care and medicines drive most household health spending.
Empanelled hospitals cluster in cities; cover without capacity cannot deliver care.
Health expenditure remains far below the **NHP 2017** target of 2.5% of GDP.
Strategic purchasing, standard treatment guidelines and fraud control determine value for money.

wf: Raise public health spending, extend cover to outpatient care and medicines, and invest in district hospitals and human resources.
gs2-47-b0.conc: Financing the demand side alone cannot buy what the supply side lacks — UHC needs public capacity as much as public insurance.

diag.foot: **PM-JAY covers hospitalisation only** · largest OOP share is outpatient · public health spend ~2% of GDP against the NHP 2017 target of 2.5%
